  [
    {
      "id": "UgzJe7jqvbDCJGCs2Qd4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "She is wrong about Leonardo not being a scientist. The goal of the work is not the work.",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UCFWx1LkmmBvXl7e0htx5HWg",
      "author": "@commonsense126",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/m2y-Rb_1NefEsjSMOUJ4ms-th7oeXMFigBUG03gHYzd9dJ5eIbfYgvFl3ffMljUFL6LJXVfCVBM=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,

      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "1 hour ago",
      "timestamp": 1776513600,
      "is_pinned": false
    },
    {
      "id": "Ugx6e1syFsJ_nLb0DUd4AaABAg",

      "text": "This is hands down THE BEST episode I've ever watched on this channel. My previous favorite was the one with Sarah Paine, but Ms. PALMER changed this.       "id": "Ugw_ZWD4QxH8HJjBqWF4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Here are more granular timestamps for the key topics discussed by Ada Palmer in the video:\n\n(0:00:00-0:16:20) The process of rediscovering Ancient Rome and the long timeline of the Renaissance.\n(0:16:20-0:22:48) How micro-technologies like footnotes and glossaries enabled broader access to ancient knowledge.\n(0:22:48-0:28:49) The shift from family-centered power networks to guild-centered structures.\n(0:28:49-0:38:13) The mechanics of Florence's unique republican government.\n(0:38:13-0:58:12) The rise of the Medici family and their influence on political power.\n(0:58:12-1:17:34) Gutenberg's economic struggles and the high financial risks of the printing industry.\n(1:17:34-1:23:02) Why Italy did not experience an industrial revolution despite early technical advancements.\n(1:23:02-1:31:02) The transition from papyrus to parchment and the historical reality of book preservation.\n(1:31:02-1:41:21) The significance of the pamphlet as a rapid information distribution medium.\n(1:41:21-2:02:20) How the Inquisition inadvertently created a form of peer review and the history of censorship.",
      "like_count": 1,
      "author_id": "UC1EOEbdyKZQEz1JF-8ADgfg",
      "author": "@aakhthuu",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/rzXJeLapxE8vjBzBclXXHN83Zh0vBevipUv5Qh752vMgy4J-667GUgoC0TgGzMMA6aVNHocJ=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

      "id": "UgxqkU4sonSMHhpdLQl4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Love this very informative. I read about Leonardo and his mirror writing. The author claims that he wasn’t hiding his writing and that mirror writing was actually a common practice at the time by left handed people because that way you wouldn’t smudge your words going left to right but rather going right to left, leaving the trail of words behind your hand as you love. It wouldn’t have been hard for anyone to figure out that his writing was backwards . From what I’ve read Leonardo failed to publish because he was too busy with his research . If only he had a useful assistant to sort out his journals, but that would be a Herculean task because he often crammed notes about different topics all on the same sheets of paper. He only had so much paper available to write on so he used every tiny bit of blank page. But the author does acknowledge that we lost centuries of progress in Da Vinci’s failure to publish.\nMy source is “Leonardo DaVinci” by Walter Isaacson",

      "id": "UgyJzpHYNWoA88TM6cJ4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Not commonly talked about in relation to the industrial revolution, but steam power and coal were more closely linked than the historian appreciates. Italy could never have developed steam power because it lacks coal.\n\nMany forms of steam power predate the industrial revolution, usually at the scale of novelty toys. The reason these designs could not scale was thermal efficiency. Very early steam engines were extremely inefficient. The first steam engines in England were used for pumping water out of coal mines. Coal mines were previously abandoned when ground water would flood them. The first steam engines had around 1% efficiency. Even reaching 5% required decades of improvements. Not only did they consume tremendous amounts of coal, only a coal mine could afford to power them because animal power was actually cheaper. Even when engines improved enough to power factories, they still relied on cheap coal. Coal fired steam engines were actually a relatively late development in coal power.",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UCZTZZwbRGEKodcmdDhcE5aQ",

      "text": "https://youtu.be/PAIhVfGbREA?t=6986 curious about this point you make about the minor theologians not being important, yet being the target of the inquisition's censorship rather than Machiavelli for your example. Do we have their works so we can see what was trying to be censored and banned? If not, maybe they were more important than we realize, and hence why they were targets of censorship. Perhaps what didn't get destroyed, or forgotten, became more important precisely because it survived. Of course we have hindsight bias of what is now looked back as important. But in their day, and in every day, the very survival of a people and of ideas is what is most important in the long run from a historical perspective. Yet something, an idea, a person or an event has to happen for the next sequential event(s) to happen, even if forgotten to history.     },
    {
      "id": "UgzLJETJlDBPfKbbvHJ4AaABAg.AV8WSor6-Z0AVfSacg54TQ",
      "parent": "UgzLJETJlDBPfKbbvHJ4AaABAg.AV8WSor6-Z0AVAmtKBbxQp",
      "text": "​ @Mazurking  There is nothing to correct. We know what village means in English, but we can find proof of what you're saying in the fact that in French, besides the word village (same meaning as in English), we also have the word ville, meaning city. So from the same source, we have two different words with completely opposite meanings. And the one that's actually consistent in form with the Latin villa isn't the one denoting a village.",
      "like_count": 1,
      "author_id": "UCLuGSbf8bdlUh9IqZ9Xkg0w",
      "author": "@jez1965",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_mhYMd8eRIZw_raiPQ_0axWm9uyydiERTzQTiAUmcLwaXTp-LIqnfZZsPeFGM2BjEvxXw=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "1 day ago",
      "timestamp": 1776470400,
      "is_pinned": false
    },
    {
      "id": "UgzLJETJlDBPfKbbvHJ4AaABAg.AV8WSor6-Z0AVhTez__1Il",
      "parent": "UgzLJETJlDBPfKbbvHJ4AaABAg.AV8WSor6-Z0AVAmtKBbxQp",
      "text": " @jez1965  \"Village\" didn't \"evolve\" from Villa, it evolved from villaggio to French \"village\" which ultimately evolved from \"villaticum\"  into \"villaggio\" and from Vllaggio to Village.\nBut in other Romance languages which English in not included, Villa actually means Village, so there's no really correct etymology of the term when it most likely had different meanings throughout the province anyway.\nso we might be going around in circles.\nBut to say \"Village\" evolved \"directly\" from Villa is also not correct.",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UCtP_ncVi0t2k-VYm_vW0W7Q",
      "author": "@gundisaluusmenendiz",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/4xhpw1GI-znNH8PyLzkJdSdPcttx5sbZjvcZoP9EOno0HLGAHEQdyzRkIeqkg70FTS4rQvvpoA=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

      "text": "I really don't like what I understand of Calvinism, which is basically \"all things that are wrong in your life, you deserve them because you are inherently lesser and there is something wrong with you\" and I realize that I don't understand very much.\n - Wait... contaminating christianity with jewish thought?       "id": "Ugxylj0cC6rO5u3Z9BZ4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Very insightful talk about the late middle ages and development of information technology. What I missed is some connection to the low countries, as they had cities and quite a large population, thus also a lot of printing and map making. Wool from England is mentioned, but a large part was made into \"Laken\" by Flemish weavers.\nI do like that trade networks in medieval times where important. Friesians where known as the long distance traders in the early middle ages and so they where the counter parts in the Italian trade. The main difference between the low countries and northern Italy is that they had much more stuff from ancient Rome laying around. Somehow clay bricks and roof tiles aren't as impressive as marble facades, although they are technically harder to make.\nOne could argue that the area that is called the bleu banana, running from northern Italy north along the rhine via the low countries to the UK midlands, isn't only the current heartland of Europe, it has been the Europe's prime region for a 1000 years and maybe longer. The start of the renaissance in Italy happens at one end of the blue area, but much happened in parallel with the rest of it.",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UCAPAgLq3axkXBzZHtqlvyUQ",

      "id": "UgzhhcRfbsqbPfnDUZd4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "0:00 The Ethical Firewall: Why Leonardo and Turing “Hid” the Future\nThe common critique of Leonardo da Vinci — that he was a scientist who “failed” the modern era because he didn’t publish — is a misunderstanding. When we compare him to Alan Turing and look through the lens of Hitler’s century, Leonardo’s secrecy looks less like failure and more like profound moral gatekeeping.\nWar as a Mandatory Muzzle\nBoth men were intellectual refugees shaped by war. Turing’s Bletchley Park work was classified by the state for national security. Leonardo, living through the Italian Wars, knew a blueprint for a tank or steam cannon wasn’t science — it was a super-weapon for the nearest warlord.\nThe Artist-Dictator Parallel\nThe 20th century gives dark justification for Leonardo’s caution. Adolf Hitler, the ultimate “failed artist,” used modern science to industrialize death. Leonardo, the supreme artist, intuitively understood the dual-use risk of his inventions. He refused to divulge designs for underwater breathing devices, fearing “the evil nature of men” would use them to sink ships and murder crews from below.\nGhost Warfare and the U-Boat Irony\nArtists have long been adept at “ghost warfare tactics” — deception, psychological shock, visual misdirection, and unconventional strategies. Leonardo essentially invented the concept of unrestricted submarine warfare 400 years early, but he hit pause because the world wasn’t morally ready.\nThe same creative impulse appeared centuries later in the WWII Ghost Army, composed of artists and designers who used inflatable tanks and sound effects to simulate entire armored divisions and deceive Nazi forces. While Leonardo restricted his designs to prevent misuse, the Ghost Army used creative deception to help end the war. In both cases, art became a tactical solution to crisis — one withheld, the other deployed.\nNot a Scientist — A Guardian\nLabeling Leonardo a “scientist” misses the point. A scientist publishes to advance the world. Leonardo was a natural philosopher and military engineer who treated knowledge as a high-stakes responsibility.\nConclusion\nLeonardo didn’t fail to help us. Like Turing, his potential was bottlenecked by the security protocols of a world at war. But unlike many who followed, Leonardo had the foresight to see that in the hands of a tyrant or a “failed artist,” his genius would have been a curse. He didn’t just write the code for the future — he acted as its first ethical firewall.",

      "id": "UgwdlpYUHwqPVUYX0WN4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "These have been some rare and amazing two hours! Reminded me a bit of the lectures of great Philippe Daverio for its multidisciplinary and realistic approach, and I miss those.\n\nI have an observation about Machiavelli's \"popolo\" referring to 4% of the people. From what I remember, Machiavelli was reasoning in a pure logic and abstract way: it takes only a few rich people, even if you are way richer than them, to be rich enough to challenge you (even if youre 8 times richer than them, it takes only 8 people, and it's not difficult for 8 people to agree on the same project), while even in great numbers people form the \"popolo\" will hardly be a menace because they are really that much below you. The totality of them, though, will most times be enough to challenge any menace against you, if they're on your side, and he proceeds with real life examples. So I don't think the percentage is relevant in this specific argument, regardless of what \"popolo\" specifically meant in those days. (Of course, in Cosimo's words, you can substitute where I wrote \"rich\" with \"rich and powerful\", probably!)\n\nAlso, I found the last part super funny, though we should want to take in account a bit of survivor bias: it's what they didn't censor that impacted the culture that was to come!",

      "parent": "root",
      "text": "She thinks that Jansenism is a trivial thing. It isn’t. It maintained that Christ did not die for all people, but only for some, and so he did not or does not love everyone.     {
      "id": "UgzUdFtMbbGpveBingJ4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Watch Da Vincis Demons (Starz). This series is the perfect blend of a high-octane thriller and a deep-dive into the human mind, making it as thought-provoking as it is entertaining. It’s essentially a \"secret history\" that uses the gaps in Leonardo da Vinci’s life to explore a massive clash between reason and religion, science and the supernatural. You’ll get a genuine history lesson on the Medici family’s grip on Florence and the corruption of the Vatican, but it’s packaged with the same intensity as a modern superhero origin story.\n\r\nThe cast is led by Tom Riley, whose performance as a young, arrogant, and restless Leonardo is absolutely magnetic—capturing both his superhuman genius and his inner \"demons\". He’s backed by a stellar ensemble, including Laura Haddock as the mysterious Lucrezia Donati and Blake Ritson as the chilling Count Riario, a villain who genuinely believes he is the hero of his own story. You’ll even see a young Nico Machiavelli (played by Eros Vlahos) before he became the famous political strategist we know today.\n\r\nBehind the scenes, the show was created and largely written by David S. Goyer, the mastermind behind The Dark Knight Trilogy and Man of Steel. Goyer treats Da Vinci like a historical Batman, applying a gritty, cinematic lens to the Renaissance. With a haunting, palindrome-based score by Bear McCreary (The Walking Dead), every episode feels like a massive, high-budget event that challenges you to rethink what you know about the past.",
      "like_count": 1,
      "author_id": "UC6AzZWM_D23JQtbMpg4GEuQ",
      "author": "@श्रीश्रीराधा",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/VNIviByUapV3__FcDc97wf6si0N6Bp8-itoB3Y0Q4odWW1hghvdToSfuMp0QsZMXcACTII3l-A=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "3 weeks ago (edited)",
      "timestamp": 1774742400,
      "is_pinned": false
    },

      "text": "Huge oversimplifications and preconceived biases not disclosed nor fully supported. The thesis that Petrarch is solely responsible for the Renaissance is a huge oversimplification.       "id": "UgxkB6ZH8-ap1g7mX8B4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Ok, rewartched, first things first: what a masterful lecture. That out of the way, on the first big question by Dwarkesh about why this causality chain narrative is correct and others aren't, which is the Skeptics traditional question, I would propose that the answer is leaving the framework, like Tolstoi proposed. The entirety of War and Peace is about this problem: \"can we talk of historical causes?\", the conclusion is \"no, we cannot.\" We can make descriptions of histories, these descriptions are accurate or inaccurate to varying degrees, they may partially overlap, etc. they may contradict or converge, and the more such descriptions you have (your data sample) the more \"accurate\" your macro description of history will be. This is not working within a falsifiable hypothesis framework (though it \"can\" include that). And then with all these descriptions generating this data space, you can start to trace co-occurrences, correlations (weaker than causation), you cannot say \"X caused Y\" like \"the printing press caused science\" (difficult claim to defend, specially if it is exclusionary of parallel \"causes\") but you can say \"the development of the printing press correlates with the development of science in a describable way\" (much easier claim to defend). It is about model building and model accuracy and it is a shift from a causality centered metaphysics to a statistical metaphysically agnostic (partially) epistemology.",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UC_BvDCDatPA8LhoD_4xvctg",

      "text": "At 1:17:10 Ada asks \"was that science\"? and the answer is a resounding yes, and almost all attributable to the invention of chemical fertilizers.",

      "id": "UgwtDH1xOsIVaj4n69h4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "I disagree with the idea that Leonardo wasn't a scientist just because he didn't 'publish' his work.( 1:09:08 - 1:11:00 )\nScience is a way of thinking, not just a social club.  Leonardo was a 'disciple of experience' who used observation and testing centuries before it was the standard.  Calling his concealment 'sabotage' ignores two important things:\nThe Inquisition made spreading radical ideas highly dangerous back then (self-preservation isn't sabotage).\nThe system of 'peer review' didn't even exist yet!\nHe wasn't failing a system; he was developing the scientific process in a world that wasn't ready for it. \nYou can’t damage a system that hasn't been born yet",
      "like_count": 3,
      "author_id": "UCrn-nXSuIT49zolPipwRDwA",

      "parent": "root",
      "text": "1:08:40 I want to correct a mistake Ada Palmer made here. She says that the vast majority of humans that have ever lived since we we were hominids have been alive in the last 200 years is incorrect. \nAccording to the Population Reference Bueau and INED, about half of all the estimated 120 to 117 billion humans to ever live (since 200,000 to 300,000 years ago) have lived in the last 2,000 to 2,500 years.\nPerhaps she read this before and had mistakenly forgotten 1 zero off of the 2,000 and made it 200, although when she says \"the vast\" this is an exaguration even from the half-of-all-humans-have-lived-in-the-last-2,000-years simplified one-liner understanding, as it is not the 'vast\" but rather just about half.",

      "id": "Ugxe29VdkQ-60Ro6yKx4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "The bit about Civilization is really interesting. I certainly came up in that milieu. I also strikingly remember talking to a professor at length about Mongol calvary tactics I learned reading the historical reference portions of Age of Empires, and the professor being like 'Why do you know this?' and me being too embarrassed to admit I learned it in a video game. I sometimes wonder at the politics of the moment we're in and whether games like AOE and Civilization have some culpability for unintentionally, and implicitly making the case to several generations of boys that managing a country/culture/civilization is easy, that a single empowered monarchical ruler can bring prosperity and/or dominance, that the masses of humanity are resources to allocate and/or exploit rather than individuals with actual rights,  and that history can be understood as a clash of cultures in a zero-sum game. I definitely feel like there's some \"thought-leaders\" in the current American rightwing movement politics (looking at you Miller, Musk and Thiel) whom one could argue approach wielding power as being something like a Civ game, and a lot of them are about the right  age and social class to have played Civ a lot as kids.",
      "like_count": 3,
      "author_id": "UCGu3MiU8dEPagh17goXxtzg",

      "text": "1:08:53 I love her talk, but she’s so wrong with this point. There is no comparison in the rate of advancement. \n\nShe’s talking about incremental increases over decades. The same advancements take months now. \n\nTake her paint example, she’s talking about advances in extraction techniques and material science improvements. \n\nThe 20’th century went from cooler looking paints, to completely synthetic pigments.       "id": "Ugyxl4l5GF6VNs6ArsJ4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "1:58:00 Here's a fun bit of astronomy trivia to go with the Kepler discussions. Often times Kepler's laws are taught with the aid of calculus and Newtonian physics. It makes them very easy to derive and to understand. But Kepler did not have calculus! He did not have Newtonian physics! Newton was born 13 years after Kepler *died*. All Kepler had to work with was Brahe's data and trigonometry. And a deep belief in heavenly perfection: perfect spheres, perfect circles, and so on. And a willingness to throw those ideas away when they did not fit Brahe's data, which is perhaps the most impressive part of all.",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UCLmaccahOK-Kdi3odmjaH0g",
      "author": "@adjsmith",

      "id": "UgxGBqytbH1BCeugdl54AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "On the topic of censorship, is it possible that miss Palmer's view is skewed by survivor's bias? Since it may very well be that the reason some of the books which have been censored aren't significant in terms of their impact on history is precisely because they were censored. Looking back, it is natural for us to say, \"Look at all of these books they censored, none of them had any real impact on the world. They missed all of the important ones.\" Isn't it possible that some of them would have revolutionized the world, had they not been censored? In other words, isn't it possible that, at least in some instances, the censorship worked? How can we know what some of those books would have done if they've been circulating?",

      "parent": "UgxWnMx6eFNdJQrj_zZ4AaABAg",
      "text": "Something I often think about, thinking about information  dissemination at 1:44:27, is that so much of our information in the \"Information Age\" exists as binaries on a computer, there will be a period after us which the international standard for digital storage is changed (this happens something like every 10 years now), and we eventually lose all this information available online, even podcasts like this one. Perhaps our descendants will think we're not well read (tbh, you could consider the modern American fairly illertate), but the reality is that we're so much so surrounded by information in the internet age, that we are quickly finding out our biology is not well suited for this environment.",

      "id": "Ugwd0dpfD_Ju8vpDiTN4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "When it comes to why industrial revolution happened in Europe, I have thought about it myself a lot too, and I think it is a mixture of a lot of factors but also one of luck. By that I mean that Roman Empire chose to spread itself up North because in part of the Sahara desert but also too strong competition in the East, that they could not conquer Parthians, so in a way they had to go for lands in a more shitty climate. Then Christianity spread Roman culture in even shittier climate, as again there was too big competition from Islam in the East... If we look around to other parts of the world, the North largely remained occupied by people who could not build significant civilizations... you had a lot of horsemen in the steppe, but not much in a sense of culture. But you need this same culture to be in the South and North for those people to compete. Like Mongols did not have same culture with the Chinese, so they just subjected Chinese and well they did not have any culture to start with so in time they settled in South and assimilated... In Europe you had Rome and you had Catholicism due to Rome and shared culture. So a king from Sweden or Netherlands may ask - why a Christian king from Constantinople or Italy is better/more wealthy than I am, and he would want to be wealthy too. But due to climate, it was impossibility if you did not invent anything - you would not be able to just outproduce Southern countries doing the same that your father did. So you needed to work your ass to get richer and use your head. While in the East crops grew much more easily and there were no harsh winters making you invest in more sophisticated homes... Also not to forget that Mongol conquest largely spared Europe, that is a big luck factor too... We see that also with Old Russian Novgorod that was in the North and was not sacked by Mongols that could develop quite sophisticated culture, but then Muscovy sacked them...\nIn other parts of the world, Northern people just did not have real sophisticated culture, never. Or let's say they did in some Northern parts of Japan or China, but those were never as fragmented in such competing but also sort of brotherly bunch of kingdoms and dutchies etc. that there was competition possible",

      "parent": "root",
      "text": "This was fascinating! I love history and this is history REAL. All the details often overlooked by other historians! What a mind she has! Would love to attend her classes! This is the first time I’ve heard this young man’s podcast and I think it’s grand there are so many younger thinkers devoted to bringing good speakers to us- so, I cannot speak to this podcast other than this one. I will comment on the podcasters speech pattern which I found difficult to follow at times in a sentence, where he suddenly speeds up his words so quickly it’s almost unintelligible- several times I did not know exactly what he said! I have noticed this cadence in other young podcasters- it appears that speed speaking is a thing with Zeds perhaps? IDK, but as Ada spoke in perfect cadence and inflected excitement  or emphasis, slowing down when appropriate! I think that made her all the more interesting to hear!       "text": "Galileo was a Scientist!  So was Leonardo da Vinci although he was more known for his paintings and his engineering abilities.       "text": "27:00 He would have been right about democracy. People who are uneducated and unsophisticated should not be electing our leaders or weighing in on important decisions. The best of both worlds.\n\n44:00 So relieved to hear Dwarkesh say the odds are \"quite low\". Today someone told me America is a police state. 😄\r\n\r\n1:05:45 What's \"Sieve\"? Link? Googling \"sieve history videogame\" turns up \"Sieve – Bananapedia, the new Super Monkey Ball Wiki\".\r\n\r\n1:10:45 \"Leonardo doesn't want to contribute to human progress.\" -- I disagree. That's like saying anyone who patents an invention \"doesn't want to contribute to human progress.\" Of course he did -- he just wanted to protect his claim and name to the inventions. He wasn't inventing things for HE ALONE to use, was he? Of course not. Speaking as an inventor, I think it's more likely that he wanted to prevent competition from his CONTEMPORARIES, rather than hide his secrets from future generations.\n\n1:12:07  I disagree. The honeybee, in your analogy, is an ENGINEER, or possibly APPLIED SCIENTIST. The spider is also an engineer, or possibly ARTIST. The one who collects information is the SCIENTIST. Science is about pure knowledge, not invention. To say the spider's web isn't \"real\" is absurd and false. That web works. Also, it didn't spring forth from the spider spontaneously -- the web material comes from high-protein food sources. You (or Bacon) are confusing teacher, inventor, and scientist. You're equating publishing research in a journal with teaching; not the same thing, at least nowadays. Sharing knowledge that OTHERS gathered is what teachers do.",

      "text": "Ehh idk about that. I studied art-art (as in the Fine Arts, oil painting), and I’d say 80% of people were there studying “just because”.       "text": " @demun6065  Nothing wrong with people not being passionate when the folks you talk about are mostly kids and extremely young adults trying to figure themselves out.     {
      "id": "Ugz7daCXaAQ9yiCOPix4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "There's one particular point where I strongly disagree with Ada, and it's honestly something that runs through her approach to history across the entire interview. \n\nThe specific point is this: \n- Around 1:55:00/1:56:00, Ada essentially argues that people in the past that censored content were almost never censoring what they \"should have\" been really worried about, the seminal texts that to us appear to be the really significant works that marked the watershed of modernity. Fair enough. \n- But what she underestimates is that for those watershed ideas to have their impact, it was first necessary to destroy the fortress of ideas that were dominant at that point in time. \n- Catholicism was that fortress in modern France, not the enlightenment, and she underestimates how appealing and strong and influential Catholic ideas were (and still are!). It was THE dominant way of thinking not just among elites but everyone in society and enlightenment ideas were really just common currency among a very small number of eccentric elites at the time, not at all widespread. Rousseau and Voltaire lived in a world that thought their ideas at best amusing and thought provoking, and mostly ridiculous. Even Voltaire is said to have written that Rousseau in his second discourse believes that humans are like dogs that walk on their hands and feet, a comment which was meant to ridicule Rousseau's ideas but today would be seen as scientifically accurate given or current evolutionary way of thinking.  \n- Even when people back then heard those ideas, they weren't much impressed because the dominant seemed more impressive and convincing. Enlightenment ideas really took hold when Catholicism had already been brutally undermined by a series of reform movements from the inside by such ideas as Jansenism and later variants. That's when materialism gained ground and even then by the 18th century people still held broadly to their religious convictions and elites embraced a kind of deism.\n- It wasn't the arrival of powerful ideas but the the destruction of the social, economic, political, and intellectual foundations of catholicism that eventually created the space for those ideas to grow at all. THAT'S WHY THEY CENSORED THOSE PROTESTANT IDEAS. THEY WERE RIGHT! THAT WAS THE THREAT TO THE DOMiNANT WORLDVIEW, NOT THE (arguably weaker) ENLIGHTENMENT VALUES THAT PLAYED SUBSTITUTE WHEN THE FORTRESS WAS DESTROYED! Ada sees those protestant critiques as unimportant because the protestants ultimately won the battle of ideas and she uncritically accepts protestant assumptions as an American from Texas.\n- Now to the broader point about her approach to history writ large: Ada has a tendency to argue that things in the past are much more similar than we think to the modern day, assume a cultural bridge between now and back then. For instance, she talks about Big Wool as an analogy to today's Big Tech, or the difficulty regulating pamphlets as similar to how it is difficult for governments to keep up with hate speech on social media. Again, fair enough. \n- However, this sometimes vastly underestimates the \"cultural\" DIFFERENCES that exist between time periods. She assumes that the works of the encyclopedists, or Voltaire, or Lucretius, or Machiavelli are inherently subversive. However, people back then were already well aware of those ideas. They just weren't respected or dominant in society, and that's mostly why they weren't in print, not because people were attracted to them, That came much later when organized religion was in free fall. In fact, she herself admits that people back then, including the inquisitors, were not worried: people aren't learned enough to get this and it's also obviously false. \n- Our starting point today, Ada's starting point, would be that these works are obviously true and significant. This is our cultural lens, which Ada fails to recognize as such. This was not true then. They weren't even significant enough to be censored. This isn't stupidity on the part of the censors. It's recognition of the real threats to the status quo that permitted later developments. \n\nTo hammer this home, what Ada is doing is analogous to this: \n- scholars 400 years from now looking back at what governments censored on social media, like people refusing to accept gender pronouns people attribute to themselves, and think: \"These people were so concerned about racist remarks back then, but they really should have been worried about what Transhumanist/Post-humanist ideas being developed in the Silicon Valley that are dominant today (i.e. using tech to transcend human limitations, attributing conscious agency to animals, plants, AI , and so on\". But in reality, we know from our vantage point today that people want to censure racist talk on social media because they are deemed a direct attack against a liberal status quo that resting on maximal tolerance and non-discrimination in the context of a democratizing and globalizing society.  It is that worldview that was dominant for decades and that worldview which once destroyed also destroys human dignity and opens up the desire to transgress human limitations, and to attribute consciousness and properly human features to non-human entities. I don't think Ada would say such censorship is really censorship because she thinks those values are relevant, and yet she judges the past like those scholars 400 years from now do, taking for granted battles of ideas that took place back then and assuming things would inevitably lead to materialism and atheism and therefore underestimating how contingent history really is! Our ideas about science and the rise of non-religious ways of seeing the world didn't HAVE to happen, and they can still go away tomorrow. \n\nRant over! :)",

      "parent": "root",
      "text": "I'm interested but a bit annoyed by her way of reducing all the topics she tackles. The main threat of all the kingdoms was division, Jansenism was one of them. It angonized the king whose purpose was to apply the 'One king, one faith, one law' idea.\nMarriages were crucial for the safety of the kingdom. They had traditions to marry princesses from allied countries. Marriages impacted the geopolitics of the time. For instance, the one between Louis XIV and Marie-Thérèse of Spain was the basis for claiming the Spanish succession, which triggered the 10 years war of the Spanish succession. Spain had been ruled by the Habsburgs of Austria until it was given to the Bourbon Philippe d'Anjou, grandson of Louis XIV.\nThere weren't so many available princesses at the time, especially Catholic ones, with the right age, in good health and originated from allied countries.\n\nThe other thing is that the society was so much built on the belief of the existence of God that imagining a disbelief was not possible. The Memoirs of St-Simon states that they didn't discuss the existence of God, they worried about what could prevent their access to paradise. The nature of the soul was a point of interrogation for instance. \n\nAnd finally, she manages to talk 2 hours about the renaissance and the life of the books without one single time mentionning the Jewish population of Florence ? \n\nThe Jews who helped Lorenzo and the Medici descendants in many ways including through providing him with rare books and manuscripts from the south of Spain, helped translating them etc... \n\nHow is that possible ?",

      "text": "1:20 \n\nThe coal aspect is really under-discussed. \n\nThe steam engine was an invention that could only exist and be profitable in an environment with large quantities of easily accessible coal and relevant use cases. \n\nEngland had easy coal reserves that let them develop an industry to mine it, which in turn led to an invention that made mining cheaper and faster, and was then applied to a large and profitable textile industry. \n\nSuch an interesting part of history.       "parent": "root",
      "text": "Oh my goodness.  What a refreshing discussion!  THIS is what I miss about having an university lecture hall of professors still.  I know most of what she is referencing but not Machiavelli’s personal contributions much so this is great.  \n     For a long while I was listening to Derek Lambert interviewing people about early  Biblical history and mythology over on Mythvision.  But for a year I have taken a break.  I was an art major who wound up taking art history classes double what I should have because an unfortunate incident made me miss my finals- so I wound up with one class with a new professor and one repeated. But other than the money wasted- I loved the classes.  It’s always great to converse or hear conversations with people who “GET” history and the interconnections of all cultures and movements and even wars. Of course art history is the best because it comes with pictures of paintings and sculptures!   \n      Many people still do not understand that we are the same as the ancients and have NOT advanced from evolution just by having more technology!  \n     I’m Native and I get colonizer mindset types still telling me that we were all “stone age” and Europeans had to “Give” us “everything.”  One guy (again like so many) tried to say Natives hadn’t invented the wheel to me.  And I rounded on him.  “First of all that is NOT true- there are examples of wheels here- But secondly WHAT HAVE YOU INVENTED?  Why do YOU get to take CREDIT for  all things someone else invented just because your skin matches theirs!?  Did YOU invent Fire?!  Why do you think pale people get to take credit for fire or wheels?  You don’t know.”  \n     Racists genuinely believe pales are more advanced and if they are Mormons- it’s part of their religious doctrine.  \n     And I loved hearing about the Florentine ways of lottery picking to keep royalty away!  I have long said we need a lottery here to get rid of the oligarchs.  It should be “Oh dang- I have to be Mayor this year!  What did you get?  Litter control district manager?  oh not too hard!  And you?  Vice President- yikes well…you can always call your mom if you need help. “",

      "id": "UgxObBvWXzMaGauF36h4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "I have 2 issues with the interpretation of Machiavelli's take on the popolos v nobles.\r\nIn the interpretation given.\r\nbeing off side with the \"Billionaires\"/Nobles, could be incredibly dangerous depending on the amount of power and influence they possess. Someone like Bezos controls significant portions of the economy and media landscape. If you sufficiently annoy someone like this, you as a governor/political leader could be in for a world of hurt as they finance your opposition and so on... which is what Elon Musk did in the last election.\r\n\r\nHowever i would interpret this differently.\n\r\nThe billionaires are not nobles, they are the popolos, millionaires and billionaires both are part of this group. they have different amounts of individual power, but the 4-5% control 90% of the wealth in the nation.\r\nIn this sense, the Nobles are in fact the political class, these are senators, presidents, or other political dynasties. You CAN do what you want to those people, because they are of minimal concern, worst they can do is vote or run against you, which wont work if you are broadly supported by the popolos. \r\nThis is i think what Machiavelli is getting at, the merchant class are (especially in Italy at the time, and today in the west generally) immensely more powerful than any individual noble and perhaps more so than most conceivable collections of nobles. \r\nWhat can the noble do about it if the banker refuses to offer him a loan and the guy who owns the blacksmith closes his doors to him.... not much. Which this i think correlates more closely with what Musk did and the threat we are supposed to perceive from being off side with the popolos.",

      "text": "Interesting bias. This is the worst time for a Palestinian or Sudanese person. The 1300’s was the best time for the Penobscot people.       "parent": "root",
      "text": "I love this. I’m getting your book. Such a good story teller. I have never heard anyone characterize the period with such clarity. I think our period is rhyming symmetrically with this period in a scary scary way - it suggests a wave pattern underlying the push and pull of causality.  Soon America will be city states, if we cannot evolve into something better. I don’t see the union holding under the crushing pressure of energy shortages and economic collapse.  Ecosystems of information and knowledge. I would say ours is in serious decline - this is the primary threat of ai. We are outsourcing skills and substituting thinking with inert simulacra. The ecosystem is failing. I suppose thinking is the last frontier - Disney, theme parks, Florida retirement communities, and cruise ships already body-snatched everything else - the whole world is Soviet, crypto-fascist kitsch now. It’s left our minds weak and ineffective at coping with a changing world. We certainly seem incapable of processing what’s happening to us. Where are all the tv shows about COVID? It’s a conspicuous absence in my opinion. We are culturally deranged. - Trumpism is fundamentally denialism: King Cnut syndrome - I command the tides to stop! Modernity is too complicated because people haven’t built an energetically efficient framework for understanding it, and so coping with it is physically exhausting and our brains are racing to make it less mentally taxing -without considering the ramifications. Ai war strategy is a spectacular/catastrophic/horrific failure. Christianity is actually having a lot of difficulty reconciling why bad things happen to good people - or rather why “good countries” are doing bad things.       "text": "Yes, yes, there's a new continent to the west, but France is about to invade now!\n\nWhat I took away from that, and I'm probably a bit predisposed to the idea, is that it's easy to get caught up in minutia of the moment, the current tempestuous teapot, and miss the things that actually matter in the long run.",

    {
      "id": "UgzAXJaLMY8OljBpxS94AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Ada Palmer mentions Petrarch, and specifically how Historical events unfolded in such a way that were totally different from what Petrarch foresaw or hoped for.\nMore intimately for the poet, was the fact that, along with Dante and Boccaccio, Petrarch is considered one of the fathers of the Italian language; something he would never have intended since Petrarch, though he started writing poetry in the Florentine dialect, he later became such a fanatical purist of Latin, that he worked in Latin till the end of his days thinking that Latin would be the commonly spoken language once again, in Italy and (he hoped) the Christian world.\nThe prank that History played on Petrarch is that it was his early domestic works in the Florentine dialect that ended up influencing the art of Poetry and the Italian language itself, while his lofty works in Latin Petrarch so highly thought of are mostly ignored curiosities even by academics.",
      "like_count": 2,
      "author_id": "UCMJ3bEW1AGyn3hgnYZhxZEw",
      "author": "@fuferito",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_n4Hg-OTIMBupTp1gIyQELI_tOO3nhHPVrtNkValU0=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "1 month ago",
      "timestamp": 1773878400,
      "is_pinned": false
    },

      "id": "UgxNlwUtfTIg_gtiEE94AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Err... I would say the honey bee is the engineer and the spider is the scientist. Ant is an academic publishing company, Elsevier for example.",

      "id": "UgzYYoKdfr7gdHonaqN4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "18:34 Actually, it was Ibn al-Nafis, a 13th-century Muslim physician, who first discovered how the heart and blood work long before Western scientists.\nNearly 300 years before William Harvey, Ibn al-Nafis correctly described pulmonary circulation, proving that blood moves from the heart to the lungs and back. He was the first to realize the heart's wall is solid and that it acts as the primary source of motion for blood, effectively identifying its role as a pump and overturning the incorrect Greek theories that the West followed for centuries.",

      "author_id": "UC0s-iIxmOMoGESn4Eboed7Q",
      "author": "@N2049-Bladerunner",

      "id": "Ugwr6LUjStmwZj7nk2l4AaABAg.AUBgOgsGtZXAUCOLrUDzGS",
      "parent": "Ugwr6LUjStmwZj7nk2l4AaABAg",
      "text": "As most of the Ancient works were saved by philosophers from the Near East.",

      "author_id": "UCDiU3--6xSvLHpj1skP3a3g",
      "author": "@Slothreadersclub",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/LdP44SnYNIY8q6LJfLjayzkIB_3A8PMHdFkGTWFQ8usq9ZM7fzUtq_ywRZRV_OoXmqTYjtnEPNg=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

    {
      "id": "Ugwr6LUjStmwZj7nk2l4AaABAg.AUBgOgsGtZXAUFfsDJyGkk",
      "parent": "Ugwr6LUjStmwZj7nk2l4AaABAg.AUBgOgsGtZXAUCOLrUDzGS",
      "text": " @Slothreadersclub  Don't you find it strikingly odd that her narrative frames the Renaissance as a kind of \"rebirth from nothing,\" completely overlooking centuries of preservation, translation, and innovation during the Islamic Golden Age and in Al-Andalus? Thinkers like Avicenna, Averroes, Al-Khwarizmi, and Ibn al-Nafis, a 13th-century Muslim physician who first understood the mechanics of the heart and blood long before Western scientists, were instrumental in shaping the very foundations upon which the Renaissance was built.\n\nNearly 300 years before William Harvey, Ibn al-Nafis accurately described pulmonary circulation, tracing blood's path from the heart to the lungs and back. He was the first to note that the heart's septum is solid, debunking earlier Greek theories still clung to in Europe, and to recognize the heart as the driving force behind blood movement, essentially identifying its function as a pump. That discovery alone should have rewritten the history books. Instead, she misattributes it to the Renaissance, erasing a monumental achievement in the process.\n\nAnd it wasn't just preservation. These scholars expanded, critiqued, and transformed Greek knowledge, then transmitted it across cultures, often via Spain and Sicily, where it flowed directly into the Italian humanist project. To begin the story in 14th-century Florence without acknowledging that intellectual pipeline is like crediting the invention of the smartphone while ignoring the discovery of electricity. The Renaissance didn't emerge from a vacuum: it stood on the shoulders of scholars who kept inquiry alive when Europe had all but extinguished it.",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UC0s-iIxmOMoGESn4Eboed7Q",
      "author": "@N2049-Bladerunner",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/i4pc5E4Kwv5wQAkDAJ10bzEsOqKhD_vvCxqADqjLn_TSBPP2cMOhwI2itU0qmOtQxxn0AWANTg=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

      "text": "A restoration bookbinder friend and I (on my prompt), tried to figure out how many sheep and goat it would take to make vellum for all the incunabula printed in Europe. Ha!       "id": "Ugw192p3qu6ltPNxrzN4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "This woman read that Gutenberg went bankrupt and decided she could fill the blanks from there. \n\nGutenberg went bankrupt because Johann Fust, the dude that lent him money to print the bibles, sued him, before he had even finished printing all the bibles. Fust claimed Gutenberg was mishandling the money and got his printshop, the press and half the bibles as collateral. He also hired Gutenberg's assistant, Peter Schöffer with whom he founded Faust & Schöffer, which immediately became a very profitable firm. So, no. The \"bank\" didn't go bankrupt, actually the opposite happened. \n\nI won't bother rectifying all the other mistakes she makes.       "id": "Ugwl7YoltfXqFX4s8NN4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Scientific method has shifted in recent decades, from the idealistic sharing for the good of humanity ethic discussed, into pressure to hold back key details of research, associate with an institution with a legal department if done as personal or small business study, and then lock down Patents, Copyrights, and other lawfare games before publishing.  \n\nEven a century ago, Edison didn't exactly play nice with Westinghouse or Tesla.  Since then, predators like Icahn or Perot set models to destroy R&D centers in industry, for short term securities scams.  \n\nAs to censorship, it might be interesting for Ada's upcoming work to consider Christopher M. Fairman's law journal article experience showing most elite lawyers are too biased to be competent in some areas of law, that evolved into a heavily end noted book, \"Fuck: Word Taboo and Protecting Our First Amendment Liberties\".       "id": "UgxUG3284R0PyCcNDc14AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "“ No, there were no widespread or universal laws prohibiting who could read the Bible at the time of Johannes Gutenberg’s invention of the movable-type printing press around 1440–1450.\nThe Gutenberg Bible itself (printed in Latin around 1455) was a Latin Vulgate edition, produced with the Church’s interest in standardizing texts for clergy and worship.       "text": "I know she knows what she's talking about cuz in 13:45 she accidentally calls Cesare Borgia \"Valentino\" and then she corrects herself and calls him just \"Cesare\".     {
      "id": "UgwTUGW9RXyIL601s7p4AaABAg.AU9RZ5zsshpAUEeAVpVm2N",
      "parent": "UgwTUGW9RXyIL601s7p4AaABAg.AU9RZ5zsshpAUAeLHkW9iU",
      "text": "​ @jones2277  there are so-called world-renowned experts with credentials from publicly-perceived-as-prestigious institutions and universities that don't know their ass from an apple, from the highest levels of government to academia.\n\nIn the past there was a much stronger link between credentialism and actual knowledge, although it was never guaranteed, due to the necessary gatekeeping and institutional hygiene. Now it is just a joke, especially in the age of \"celebrity academics\".\n\nThe letters next to someone's name, the fact that they have books published, or anything else really tell you nothing about the authenticity of their expertise, only that they knew how to fillet - literally were metaphorically that's the right people. Only once you actually look into their work, or hear them run their mouth for a while consistently, can you get some idea of what they actually know.\n\nThis is an unfortunate reality, but the inevitable result of trying to \"democratize knowledge\" fused with instant telecommunications and the attention economy",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UC6kSgmFt9_VmuEVt9CYXnvA",
      "author": "@Laotzu.Goldbug",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/N9r89-GOYk4HpZbOcpWaly7vBy0uTOrBzhNOD2j5EBMDzTn3F0RsiMr7HmYATu__8HD_phtKwA=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

      "parent": "UgwTUGW9RXyIL601s7p4AaABAg.AU9RZ5zsshpAUAeLHkW9iU",
      "text": "​ @jones2277 how about i didnt know her in advance and it was only 13 minutes in? Also, shes not a world renowned expert in the field, she just published her third book on it, its not a niche subject, three books are not enough, James Hankins has like 30 volumes on it.",

      "author": "@fkfnfndjdikdkd-qk6cv",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_mA2AVFV-qavNRylO-8a4Gy-Z6PmCR1F_ZClH9D2RWiGO4aLpoBwvnFubP3fe06ChSeLA=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

    {
      "id": "UgwTUGW9RXyIL601s7p4AaABAg.AU9RZ5zsshpAUdBtr3qBDw",
      "parent": "UgwTUGW9RXyIL601s7p4AaABAg.AU9RZ5zsshpAUC4Bh66G3u",
      "text": "@fkfnfndjdikdkd-qk6cv  IMO being the editor of a volume or journal is more indicative of one's status in a field than how many monographs you've published. especially with popular topics you can find scholars who publish a book every couple years. at least in my experience those books have little historiographical consequence. being an editor shows historiographical engagement and prestige in a field which is way more important than spines on a shelf. \n\nedit - also since she was tenure track at uchicago, after finishing her first book she was in no hurry to publish. she took plenty of time on her second book which I think is wonderful. there's a reason uchicago has such a reputation for producing impactful work (sometimes simply by merit of coming from uchicago, which is a detriment on occasion).",

    {
      "id": "Ugxopk2QezZXT9-6aht4AaABAg.AU8HiOngAw6AUnCud3ufj3",
      "parent": "Ugxopk2QezZXT9-6aht4AaABAg",
      "text": "I agree that he is an excellent interviewer, and I really enjoy this channel. It's curious how often I read this comment, however. Who are you all people watching that interrupt all the time? Like why are you watching them if that's the case?",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UCBWqwc3L_z8pIvzzDmBhDRA",
      "author": "@Rhymes-and-Reasons",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/77Fev5h6qiMEDmPeHoVB75xz4oDdTE70Lg0Tao8ZrcIPaNl0U3sdf9Q8DyvsjAo3Mvd-f3fvhig=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "3 weeks ago",
      "timestamp": 1774742400,
      "is_pinned": false
    },
    {
      "id": "Ugxopk2QezZXT9-6aht4AaABAg.AU8HiOngAw6AUnHlsa7has",
      "parent": "Ugxopk2QezZXT9-6aht4AaABAg",
      "text": "That's the difference between \"performative\" conversation and \"private\" conversation (I'm using these terms casually, to talk about this, there's no broader theory):\n\nin \"private\" conversations, which are aimed at coming to consensus, discussing, conversing...interruption can be massively helpful and supporting.\n\nThe worst miscommunication is arguably when listeners don't understand while the speaker keeps going on.\n\nThen, when they finally pause, they find out others haven't been following at all.\n\nNot only does this waste everyone's time, but it confuses the conversation for everyone, especially the speaker, who no longer has any sense of what's been understood or not.\n\nThere is no perfect compromise between allowing trains of thought to flow, and making sure communication is actually happening.\n\nFor performative conversations meant to be listened to by others,\n\ninterruptions make no sense. Any interruption that would be aimed at helping listeners follow along, can be better directed at asking questions to shift the conversation to be better aimed at them.\n\nInterrupting serves the interests of limited individuals who are tailoring communication to the present moment.\n\nThere is no need for it when tailoring communication for the masses in the future.\n\nI find it maddening when folks refuse to interrupt me, and listen silently.\n\nOften, I find this makes it impossible for us to communicate. I need them to be monitoring whether they're following me, and stopping me when I've begun talking to a brick wall.\n\nUnfortunately, in most modern communication, people don't want to know how much of what they're saying has been understood as intended. Most of our speech is not seeking understanding. People widely focus primarily on the superficial aspects of language.\n\nIn rhetoric, meaning doesn't matter—only convincing others. Since we use language MUCH more to come to agreement and to argue and reason rather than to seek truth, reality, or understanding,\n\nthose are the most salient meanings of language. The superficial always-untrue heuristic \"wrong but useful\" connotations dominate, and become what a \"reasonable\" person can be expected to focus on.\n\nThe language ends up affecting thinking and reinforcing these loops.\n\nEnglish is such an awful language for true communication...it is great for rhetoric and politics, though. It's good for talking about stuff.\n\nSaying anything in English requires one to consider when what they're saying is taking place. It's impossible to speak or think in the language without taking time for granted, and treating the illusion of it as real.\n\nOr course this is basically limiting.\n\nThe solutions exist. Some other languages allow for making statements which have no specified relationship to time.",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UCDSEZm87puTb3Bhsn8bTX7Q",
      "author": "@davidf2244",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_ksfdpRZpPs4j6fyF5N-klaC5V0f4T5RnerYlg6D6U=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

      "parent": "root",
      "text": "2:50 you forgot roman bishops seizing control of roman cities and the surrounding region by hiring - and baptising - 'barbarian' strongmen. This happened all along the limes. The church naturally filled the spot the roman magistrates left, they didn't feel the need to obey any 'roman general' telling them they should return to italy, because they weren't guarded any longer, but saw it as a fact, that it was their mission by god to uphold christendom and no roman magister militum could contest a mission given by god, a - soon self-titled 'prince-bishop' - had decided to uphold. This - and the fact that these bishops occasionally (unless they died in office) took with advancing age-related frailty their favourite readings from their 'city-libraries' to their pensioneers seats (that was often choosen to be an abbey) led to findings like those of Poggio Bracciolini.",

      "parent": "UgzM2hcRH7RuxECH7dp4AaABAg",
      "text": "They're only inconsequential because we have 20/20 hindsight.   No one knows what we invent today that will last 1000 years",

    {
      "id": "UgzM2hcRH7RuxECH7dp4AaABAg.AU5t4IRjEUsAU7It7SS6Xw",
      "parent": "UgzM2hcRH7RuxECH7dp4AaABAg.AU5t4IRjEUsAU7FWI1nwwW",
      "text": "​​ @andygoody2599 If humankind is alive after 1000 years, they still absolutely will view the jump from the Wright brothers plane to Apollo program as enormous, just like we view the invention of the Gutenberg press as very significant. And getting back to the Roman steam engine example - no one viewed it as particularly important at any point in history, including in contemporary times.\nI'm not arguing that humans were less ingenious back then, but it was much harder for them to gain knowledge and to spread the new knowledge that they gained, which made knowledge work extremely inefficient. Adding to that, there were much fewer humans that could even afford the \"leisure\" of knowledge work. There's absolutely no way these two factors (among others) would not have slowed the rates of technological progress compared to modern times, so anyone claiming that they were in fact the same would have to present some extraordinary evidence in favor of their hypothesis, not just \"they were inventing stuff all the time\"",
      "like_count": 0,

      "text": "I can read a comment on Ada Palmer's book, \"Too Like the Lightning\". The narrator of this book is fantastic and audible.       "text": "Lovely conversation, thank you. But it never ceases to amaze me how few scholars of the renaissance put the stress in “Medici” on the right ie first syllable. They were originally, before they became bankers, medical people - medics, not meDicks:-)",

      "parent": "UgwE20Y8QxJYksLH4xp4AaABAg.AU2RdW8smiBAU8arc8m9In",
      "text": "​@mirekcolakov1730 that's not how historians have agreed to use pronunciation. The agreed form is to use the word that is most easily understood/recognisable. Thats why we say Medici as she has said. Because not everyone will understand and thus you will limit youe reach.",

      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_mNEAv5MPjwUYT_oMN-I_oKxZXRDcwTzQ5m2dLC8BLZIN_r2XL_arB8rM0NkGGWBLQJXQ=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

    {

      "parent": "UgwE20Y8QxJYksLH4xp4AaABAg.AU2RdW8smiBAUYs9JxSHgd",
      "text": " @Madsixseven I disagree. What’s the point of adopting a word from different language and messing up its pronunciation. It is laziness if you ask me, unwillingness to learn other languages…",
      "like_count": 2,
      "author_id": "UCp6M71CbANSFFftoLMmzFWQ",
      "author": "@mirekcolakov1730",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_lrYP-XuLdgmiVhR_qRSgP4bI2x-40H71HMsPaSIuU=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

    {
      "id": "UgwE20Y8QxJYksLH4xp4AaABAg.AU2RdW8smiBAUmQIA9Pg-S",
      "parent": "UgwE20Y8QxJYksLH4xp4AaABAg.AU2RdW8smiBAUYs9JxSHgd",
      "text": " @mirekcolakov1730  Applied linguist here. It's not really about laziness per se. While I think of preserving/using the source-language pronunciation as a sign of respect (and fun!), it is perfectly natural for borrowed words (as linguists call them) and names to be assimilated to the receiving group's sound system. Stress on the second syllable feels more comfortable for English-speakers because of our usual rhythm, stress, and sound patterns. --- Americans don't get upset when Italians say English words or names in an Italian way, especially when they're speaking in Italian. Trying to get an Italian (or French, or Chinese, or Swahili...) speaker to change how they say something to match an American (or British, or Australian...) accent while speaking that other language would even seem offensive in many cases. Also, humans tend to repeat whatever we heard first. And that's generally fine, even if it's different from the way other groups say it.",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UCmmQ0I9U52PhUab2KzJxxsg",
      "author": "@lindareed8265",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_mzE7jxxRVYWTfHcAmklCerhdQjL2bpFoSTV95Cp8qJptg=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

      "text": "​ @mirekcolakov1730  Applied linguist here. While I think of preserving/using the source-language pronunciation as a sign of respect (and fun!), it is perfectly natural for borrowed words (as linguists call them) and names to be assimilated to the receiving group's sound system. Americans don't get upset when Italians say English words in an Italian way, especially when they're speaking in Italian. Trying to get an Italian (or French, or Chinese, or Swahili...) speaker to change how they say something to match an American (or British, or Australian...) accent would even seem offensive in many cases. Humans tend to repeat whatever we heard first. And that's generally fine, even if it's different from the way other groups say it.",

      "text": "Very well observed. Exactly. Intellectual humility: a mind formidable enough to dominate, yet so self-effacing that it fell silent in the presence of another’s insight,  broad and pursuasing, as a huge river.",

      "text": "​​ @tykidides  I like your huge river analogy but if I may so critique, your use of self-effacing doesn't quite work. Self-effacing is something one does actively: a joke about one's self. So if you're silent you're not being self-effacing.\n\n \"so humble\" works better. Or even better \"humble enough that\" \n\nWhen writing eloquently you have to be ready to use the simpler word if it's more accurate to the meaning being conveyed. And what this ends up doing is providing support for when impressive words really do hit.",

      "text": " @IntricateJason a genuinely “extremely smart” person would know when they’re in the presence of someone smarter and shut up.       "author": "@Heyimpara",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/iQyyYgdLL892VUo_nFPCnqnlEYdFjSmVVAwQxHcrMqwjUrCq933fTq7wyqaB5EQJ3heVpQ5SUqM=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

    {
      "id": "UgwE20Y8QxJYksLH4xp4AaABAg.AU2RdW8smiBAUDxJeGYAB6",
      "parent": "UgwE20Y8QxJYksLH4xp4AaABAg.AU2RdW8smiBAUD61I9gS-Y",
      "text": "​ @Heyimpara I disagree. That js about conditioning, rather than being smart. He is curious and therefore asks questions and shares his own views. And if what the other person says is not interesting enough, he tries takes over to correct the course of the conversation. Of course he knows these people are smart and know more about their specialties than he does, he is not stupid enough to not realize that. But if the speaker is not eloquent enough in expressing that knowledge, Dwarkesh starts asking questions or proposing his own ideas to get a reaction beceause that helps him understand faster. I do that too and it is mostly unconcious. It is with speakers like Ada Palmer that the story is already so fascinating that Dwarkesh has little to add. But if the speaker is not explaining things in a way he understands, he steps in. It is a sign of curiosity",
      "like_count": 16,
      "author_id": "UC9jcWpP4zP17ZpFoNlYeQmA",

      "parent": "UgwE20Y8QxJYksLH4xp4AaABAg.AU2RdW8smiBAUD61I9gS-Y",
      "text": " @Heyimpara  I have to disagree, I've met countless people with extremely high IQ and many of them don't know humility. It's wise people that know how to listen, not smart people, and wisdom has no known relation to intelligence.",

      "parent": "UgwE20Y8QxJYksLH4xp4AaABAg.AU2RdW8smiBAUD61I9gS-Y",
      "text": " @Heyimpara  I think he learns through debating a topic. You can gain a lot of insight by proposing an alternative opinion and letting that person dismantle why it doesn’t work.  You gain lot more information by challenging it than if you just let someone explain their point of view.  The challenge of their opinion results in discussing the nuances. It allows the person to steel man what they they’re saying, which is a really common technique. \n\nI don’t find him combative, I find him curious and pushing the interviewer to steel man their position. While he may not be an expert, but he does a lot of background knowledge to know what other people in the field are saying that are contradicting the guest and he’s just bringing those the opposing opinions.",

      "text": "​ @Kameleron21  yes, I do in fact instantly understand most things. It goes further.       "parent": "root",
      "text": "I have always thought the industrial revolution happened in England (western Europe) rather than Italy was the discovery and colonialization of the Americas. Because like she was saying about how the expense of paper and parchment caused Gutenberg to go bankrupt, if a seemingly limitless access of land and therefore the limitless growth and/or extraction of raw material creates the motivation of processing and creating larger amounts of cheaper products exists in one of the few moments of history. ## Description

Renaissance history is so much wilder and weirder than you would have expected. Very fun chatting with Ada Palmer (historian, novelist, and composer based at the University of Chicago).

Some especially fascinating things I learned from the conversation and her excellent book, Inventing the Renaissance: https://a.co/d/03EjyByR

We're very accustomed in the modern period to thinking of the government as being our big safety net. If we wonder who is going to fund the hospitals, whose job is it to

take care of orphans, we think of the government, or maybe the church. But in this period, if you're killed and you leave orphans behind, it is your employer whose

duty it is to take care of them. If you are injured and can no longer work, it is your employer who will support you for the rest of your life while you are disabled and find you work

that you can do with that disability. A huge portion of the safety net is your employer. Are you in trouble with the law? Your employer will supply

your defense attorney. Your employer will supply the persuasive note to the judge that they would very much appreciate if their person got off. This is the system known as the patronage

system, and it existed in ancient Rome. It exists and saturates the medieval and the Renaissance worlds in which everyone is in a very interconnected hierarchy. So if you're a brewer and your son

gets in a barroom brawl and punches somebody out and the person's nose breaks and they die in the brawl and your son is suddenly in trouble and you say, "Oh no, I don't want my son to be

executed," you turn to your landlord. Your landlord turns to his landlord. They turn to one of these major families. These major families are massive landowners that own dozens of

apartments within the city. Hundreds or thousands of people work for them. So it makes sense to everyone to be represented that way, like having

a council of the CEOs of all of the organizations that employees work for, when your corporation also supplies your social safety net and you see your representation there.

It's also a world that's used to thinking in terms of hierarchy and very unused to thinking about real democracy. It really doesn't have any confidence in what we would recognize as democracy.

We talk about these republics, and we're very excited by the fact that they give more power to the people than a monarchy does, but they're still incredibly narrow oligarchic republics.

When we read Machiavelli, he talks a lot about the popolo, which we translate as "the people." He talks about how important it is that the popolo are respected and have a

This feels like documents of the founding of the US where we're respecting and arming and trusting the people." Popolo meant the top 4% economically of the population,

the members of the merchant guilds. That's the popolo. He's talking about a narrow-slice oligarchy being heard, a narrow-slice oligarchy being respected.

of the period and realize how people use these words. Florence in this period goes through five different forms of government. It's this republic of nine

office in the Florentine Republic. To us, we look at it and say, "It's a long red robe. It looks very Renaissance." To them, it looked like a toga because of the way it was draped.

They thought of this as a toga. They're cosplaying the Roman Republic. Wearing a Florentine toga while in office was something that you did to represent your fealty to

Cicero and republican values. The dukes made their men continue to wear these. In fact, the first Duke, Cosimo I, would wear one to costume balls as if in his

It's sort of doubly ironic that they are doing the same thing, but in the 1500s. And it means that more rights are granted to the people of Florence than to other cities that fell

to monarchies at similar points. The monarchs of Florence know they have to be careful, they have to respect rights to a certain amount, and they can't run roughshod over them.

There's a really cool building that I love in Florence. If you've been there, there's the famous bridge, the Ponte Vecchio, which has little jeweler shops all along it.

When you get to the end of it, there's this funny overhead corridor, the Vasari Corridor, which was built by the dukes of Florence to connect the old city palace where the senate used to meet—where they

had to have their seat of power—to their new palace across the river, which was much bigger, where they could have grand balls and things that dukes need to have. Because they're so terrified of being

assassinated by their own people, they built this overhead walkway that goes from one end of the city to the other so that they could walk in safety without being assassinated.

This is a sign of a weak duke. But also, when he was building it, it's going across the roofs and sometimes blasting off the second stories of different people's houses.

Most people, when His Grace the Duke says, "I'm gonna blast the top story off your house," would say, "Yes, Your Grace, please continue." There are literally severed heads of

people who resisted still rotting on spikes in front of the Palazzo Vecchio. But they get to this one point where there's a very old tower, a 500-year-old tower.

This belongs to the Mannelli family, who are descended from peers of Julius Caesar and can trace their genealogy all the way back to an old Roman gens. When the duke says, "We want to

knock the top off your tower," they say, "No, this is our tower. This tower has been ours since before the Medici existed as a named family. You may not knock the top off."

And the duke does not knock the top off. The corridor goes around in this awkward square around that tower, because he knows that if he violates something as traditional and core to

the civilization as the property rights of somebody who has owned something for a long time, there will be rebellion, civil war, dissent, and resistance. These are monarchs who know that

they are weak and are therefore careful, and therefore more rights, like property rights, exist. Meanwhile, across the river in Ferrara, Duke Alfonso I d'Este of Ferrara used
