and Hungary and might be coming again. Also over there, there's a new thing. Okay, great. We'll worry about that when we're not having three wars at the same time.

But guys, we're having three wars at the same time. Oh my God. And then Martin Luther hits Europe like a ton of bricks when they still

haven't even figured out that this is a continent and not an island. In the same way, if you're in a country and it's having a tumult, you worry a lot about its tumult, even if a larger

tumult is happening in a faraway country. It's hard to bring your mind out of Europe at crisis to be like, "Hey, this is a thing." The other is they're inventing

lots of new things, and it falls into the sphere along the rest. They're discovering the existence of sub-Saharan Africa, where they thought there was basically one

country's worth of stuff, south of the Sahara, Ethiopia and nothing else. Then they're like, "Oh my God, there's a whole big thing that sticks out." They're also discovering

that the heart is a pump. That's a bit later, but they're discovering all sorts of stuff at the same time. The discovery of the New World,

especially when they realize how big it is, becomes an intellectual challenge where they say, "Wait, does this mean all the maps we've had are wrong? Does this mean the ancients

were wrong about geography? Does it mean the world is a lot bigger than we used to think the world is? Let's worry about that the same way we worry about revolutionizing our

mathematics and figuring out that the sun doesn't go around the Earth." These are things that are paradigm shifting. But on the other hand, does it matter

whether the sun goes around the Earth or the Earth around the sun when the French are invading right now and we need to get the defenses going, and there's a giant civil war happening,

and we're about to be betrayed? It does matter, but it also doesn't matter. Any decade is concerned by its tumults and often fails to recognize

the importance of what's around it. That’s true of every decade. One fun game when I study the history of censorship, which I work a lot on—my next non-fiction book is

gonna be a book on the history of censorship—whatever they're looking at, they're always wrong, from our perspective, about what they should be worried about censoring.

If we had a time machine and our goal is to go give them advice… Here we are in the French Enlightenment, Voltaire and Rousseau and the Marquis de Sade and La Mettrie's articulations of materialist

atheism are flying around Europe. What is the Inquisition worried about? It's worried about Jansenist treatises about the nature of the Trinity. Jansenism is sort of like a

Calvinist version of Catholicism. Do you want to have an incredibly terrifying authoritarian God who hates you and tells you that your soul is a worthless spider that deserves to

be hurled into fire, but also have to obey the arbitrary pope in Rome? Then Jansenism is for you. It has all the grimness of Calvinism and all of the authoritarian

centrality of the Roman Catholics. This was a heresy that was abroad in the Enlightenment, and they are so much more worried about Jansenism than they are about Voltaire.

Remember that very chapter in Matytsin's book I mentioned where they are raiding the clandestine bookshop. They're like, "Voltaire, fine. The banned Encyclopédie, which is gonna

revolutionize all thought in Europe, fine. letters of Diderot, Rousseau, fine, fine. Jansenist treatises about the nature of the Trinity! Throw the book at these guys!

This is the worst thing!" They really are obsessed with this incredibly petty minor heresy to the degree that when the Encyclopédie is banned by Rome… France likes the Encyclopedia.

This is Diderot and d’Holbach’s big project of universal education, to print an encyclopedia that will collect all world knowledge. They articulate it as, "Should a

new dark age come upon humankind and even one copy of the encyclopedia survive, it will be sufficient to reconstruct all human progress." That's the goal of this thing.

It's advancing incredibly radical ideas about biology, about statecraft, about reforming the law to be rational instead of traditional, all sorts of stuff. When that is banned by Rome, Paris is

commanded... Paris loves this book. The king likes this book. The queen likes this book. She's on record saying it was so cool being able to look up the technology

that was used to make her silk pantyhose. She just loves it. Everybody loves it. France allows it to circulate despite its controversial content.

But Rome says, "No, you must ban this book." So they agree they're gonna have the ceremonial burning, and they march the Encyclopédie up to the fire.

Then they get some Jansenist treatise about the nature of the Trinity and burn those instead, because they don't want to burn the Encyclopédie. They love it.

They want to burn this other thing. This is always true. If we had a time machine for the Inquisition in the 1540s, we would say, "Guys, Machiavelli, he's really

important. He's really revolutionary. You gotta be looking at this." Or we would say Lucretius's De rerum natura, which I did my dissertation on… Many people are familiar with

Greenblatt's book, The Swerve, which credits a lot of change to the materialist science that this poem articulates. There's a much more complex story, which you know is told in my book,

which refers to Greenblatt's. If anyone enjoyed The Swerve, you would really enjoy the more detailed zoom-in that Inventing the Renaissance has. But we would say, "Guys,

you should censor this." We literally have letters of inquisitors writing to each other saying, "We don't need to bother censoring Lucretius. Only learned people can read it,

and they know perfectly well that the false stuff is false, so it'll just circulate and it's fine. What we need to worry about censoring is all of these fine

minutiae of Protestantism." The 1545 edition of the Index of Banned Books says in its introduction, "We shall put the names of arch-heretics in all caps."

When I first read that, I was like, "Ooh, I want to see all my favorite arch-heretics be in all caps." I eagerly flip to M, and Machiavelli is not in all caps.

He was not important enough from their position. The all caps authors are all minor Protestant theologians. They're all people like Calvin and

Zwingli and Luther and Melanchthon. They're all doing stuff that we would say does not matter. But an era is always wrong about what ideas and what circulation and what

changes are the really big ones and are always much, much more worried about, "Oh my God, the Prince of Spain, which princess is he gonna marry? This is going to determine whether

Spain is or isn't annexed by Germany. This is the most important thing that has ever happened in the entire stream of time." People are like, "We've

discovered another continent," and they're like, "We don't care. We just wanna know who's gonna marry Charles." That's a very profound observation.

It was really interesting to learn from your book that of all the thousands of people killed during the Inquisition, one guy was executed for atheism. Science-related stuff.

And even he had these ideas of reincarnation or... I think probably the number executed for atheism would be about 100. There are 12 total trials

of scientists about science. Galileo is one. Giordano Bruno is one. Giordano Bruno is the only one executed. Of those 12 trials, only

three were convicted. Hundreds of thousands of trials for Judaizing, which is theoretically contaminating Christianity with Jewish thought, and all of these

other minutiae of oppression and segregation of populations, executions for paganism, meaning practicing your indigenous religion in a colonized space… Hundreds of thousands of

executions for that, one for science. I recently got interested in the story of Kepler just because the way he discovers the laws of planetary motion is so whimsical

with the theory of Platonic objects. While he's going through Brahe's data and coming up with the laws of planetary motion, he is the imperial mathematician for the Habsburg

emperor, which basically means that he's doing astrology for a general. Will we win the battle or whatever. Then he gets excommunicated, not for the laws of planetary motion,

but because he's a Lutheran. In fact, his mother is tried for witchcraft. Again, has nothing to do with science, it’s just because she's also a Lutheran.

Milton of Paradise Lost fame wrote our first big defense of the free press. This is in the moment in the early 1600s when England doesn't yet have systematic censorship law.

It has ad hoc, "Hey, this book is bad," but it doesn't have systematic, "You must submit all books to a censor," the way the Catholic world does by that point. The Catholic world developed it

in order to fight Protestantism. There's a lot of support for creating censorship in England at the time because there's anxiety about Papists plotting against our nice non-Catholic

country, trying to undermine it. There's a general feeling of anxiety. There's also deliberate moral panic whipped up by politicians and power-seeking people

who whip up a deliberate moral panic about books, the same way in 1954 there was a moral panic about comic books or the same way there was a moral panic about Dungeons &amp; Dragons in the '90s.

There's a moral panic about scary and dangerous books and pamphlets. So there's a movement to create state censorship for the first systematic time in England.

Milton writes this big treatise about why freedom of the press is important, the Areopagitica. It’s a beautifully written rhetorical piece that presents the

importance of how we must trust truth to rise purely to the top. We must let free voices move, otherwise you're gonna create a situation where people are writing for the censor

first and for the public second. It will constrain people's thoughts in the way that we know chilling effects and fear do. It's a beautiful treatise.

He fails. The censorship regime passes. Paradise Lost is published under the censorious regime. It goes through the censorship.

The one line they tell him to change is about astrology. They're like, "It's perfectly fine having Satan be your charismatic protagonist and God be kind of a

jackass, and also having Satan spout ferocious anti-monarchical rhetoric copied from revolutionary pamphlets that are circulating in the British colonies so that he's actually parroting

republican, anti-monarchical rhetoric, very dangerous stuff in the treatise. That's fine. But this one line about a comet causing a thing to happen, no, no, no.

Astrology is gonna confuse people's souls." You're like, "Guys, speaking as a time traveler, you're so wrong about what you're censoring." They always are.

You have one sentence which I couldn't trace down, which I found very interesting. You said, "In the late 17th century, the most extensive library in

all of Europe is the one in the Vatican run by the inquisitors." Not the library, the most extensive experimental laboratory. Daniele

Macuglia is the scholar there. That's from his dissertation. I think it's been published now, but I don't know if it's actually out in English.

It's out in Italian. He works on the Inquisition and the immediate aftermath of Galileo. They saw themselves as guarantors of truth and of accuracy in information.

So they decided after Galileo that they had a duty to verify the truth of the books that they were sent to censor. If people were going to be doing mechanical experiments, they needed

to repeat the mechanical experiments to see whether they were true. So they effectively invented peer review, which is to say they invented a second laboratory trying to

recreate the results of the first. There are these amazing people who by day are inquisitors and by night are going home to write their own scientific treatises as they do these experiments.

It's not what we expect, but history is never what we expect. Seems like a good place to close. Ada, thank you very much. Thank you.

> (0:28:49-0:38:13) The mechanics of Florence's unique republican government.
> (0:38:13-0:58:12) The rise of the Medici family and their influence on political power.
> (0:58:12-1:17:34) Gutenberg's economic struggles and the high financial risks of the printing industry.
> (1:17:34-1:23:02) Why Italy did not experience an industrial revolution despite early technical advancements.
> (1:23:02-1:31:02) The transition from papyrus to parchment and the historical reality of book preservation.
> (1:31:02-1:41:21) The significance of the pamphlet as a rapid information distribution medium.
> (1:41:21-2:02:20) How the Inquisition inadvertently created a form of peer review and the history of censorship.

> Not commonly talked about in relation to the industrial revolution, but steam power and coal were more closely linked than the historian appreciates. Italy could never have developed steam power because it lacks coal.
> 
> Many forms of steam power predate the industrial revolution, usually at the scale of novelty toys. The reason these designs could not scale was thermal efficiency. Very early steam engines were extremely inefficient. The first steam engines in England were used for pumping water out of coal mines. Coal mines were previously abandoned when ground water would flood them. The first steam engines had around 1% efficiency. Even reaching 5% required decades of improvements. Not only did they consume tremendous amounts of coal, only a coal mine could afford to power them because animal power was actually cheaper. Even when engines improved enough to power factories, they still relied on cheap coal. Coal fired steam engines were actually a relatively late development in coal power.

> 0:00 The Ethical Firewall: Why Leonardo and Turing “Hid” the Future
> The common critique of Leonardo da Vinci — that he was a scientist who “failed” the modern era because he didn’t publish — is a misunderstanding. When we compare him to Alan Turing and look through the lens of Hitler’s century, Leonardo’s secrecy looks less like failure and more like profound moral gatekeeping.
> War as a Mandatory Muzzle
> Both men were intellectual refugees shaped by war. Turing’s Bletchley Park work was classified by the state for national security. Leonardo, living through the Italian Wars, knew a blueprint for a tank or steam cannon wasn’t science — it was a super-weapon for the nearest warlord.
> The Artist-Dictator Parallel
> The 20th century gives dark justification for Leonardo’s caution. Adolf Hitler, the ultimate “failed artist,” used modern science to industrialize death. Leonardo, the supreme artist, intuitively understood the dual-use risk of his inventions. He refused to divulge designs for underwater breathing devices, fearing “the evil nature of men” would use them to sink ships and murder crews from below.
> Ghost Warfare and the U-Boat Irony
> Artists have long been adept at “ghost warfare tactics” — deception, psychological shock, visual misdirection, and unconventional strategies. Leonardo essentially invented the concept of unrestricted submarine warfare 400 years early, but he hit pause because the world wasn’t morally ready.
> The same creative impulse appeared centuries later in the WWII Ghost Army, composed of artists and designers who used inflatable tanks and sound effects to simulate entire armored divisions and deceive Nazi forces. While Leonardo restricted his designs to prevent misuse, the Ghost Army used creative deception to help end the war. In both cases, art became a tactical solution to crisis — one withheld, the other deployed.
> Not a Scientist — A Guardian
> Labeling Leonardo a “scientist” misses the point. A scientist publishes to advance the world. Leonardo was a natural philosopher and military engineer who treated knowledge as a high-stakes responsibility.
> Conclusion
> Leonardo didn’t fail to help us. Like Turing, his potential was bottlenecked by the security protocols of a world at war. But unlike many who followed, Leonardo had the foresight to see that in the hands of a tyrant or a “failed artist,” his genius would have been a curse. He didn’t just write the code for the future — he acted as its first ethical firewall.

> Watch Da Vincis Demons (Starz). This series is the perfect blend of a high-octane thriller and a deep-dive into the human mind, making it as thought-provoking as it is entertaining. It’s essentially a "secret history" that uses the gaps in Leonardo da Vinci’s life to explore a massive clash between reason and religion, science and the supernatural. You’ll get a genuine history lesson on the Medici family’s grip on Florence and the corruption of the Vatican, but it’s packaged with the same intensity as a modern superhero origin story.
> 
> The cast is led by Tom Riley, whose performance as a young, arrogant, and restless Leonardo is absolutely magnetic—capturing both his superhuman genius and his inner "demons". He’s backed by a stellar ensemble, including Laura Haddock as the mysterious Lucrezia Donati and Blake Ritson as the chilling Count Riario, a villain who genuinely believes he is the hero of his own story. You’ll even see a young Nico Machiavelli (played by Eros Vlahos) before he became the famous political strategist we know today.
> 
> Behind the scenes, the show was created and largely written by David S. Goyer, the mastermind behind The Dark Knight Trilogy and Man of Steel. Goyer treats Da Vinci like a historical Batman, applying a gritty, cinematic lens to the Renaissance. With a haunting, palindrome-based score by Bear McCreary (The Walking Dead), every episode feels like a massive, high-budget event that challenges you to rethink what you know about the past.

> Ok, rewartched, first things first: what a masterful lecture. That out of the way, on the first big question by Dwarkesh about why this causality chain narrative is correct and others aren't, which is the Skeptics traditional question, I would propose that the answer is leaving the framework, like Tolstoi proposed. The entirety of War and Peace is about this problem: "can we talk of historical causes?", the conclusion is "no, we cannot." We can make descriptions of histories, these descriptions are accurate or inaccurate to varying degrees, they may partially overlap, etc. they may contradict or converge, and the more such descriptions you have (your data sample) the more "accurate" your macro description of history will be. This is not working within a falsifiable hypothesis framework (though it "can" include that). And then with all these descriptions generating this data space, you can start to trace co-occurrences, correlations (weaker than causation), you cannot say "X caused Y" like "the printing press caused science" (difficult claim to defend, specially if it is exclusionary of parallel "causes") but you can say "the development of the printing press correlates with the development of science in a describable way" (much easier claim to defend). It is about model building and model accuracy and it is a shift from a causality centered metaphysics to a statistical metaphysically agnostic (partially) epistemology.

> I disagree with the idea that Leonardo wasn't a scientist just because he didn't 'publish' his work.( 1:09:08 - 1:11:00 )
> Science is a way of thinking, not just a social club.  Leonardo was a 'disciple of experience' who used observation and testing centuries before it was the standard.  Calling his concealment 'sabotage' ignores two important things:
> The Inquisition made spreading radical ideas highly dangerous back then (self-preservation isn't sabotage).
> The system of 'peer review' didn't even exist yet!
> He wasn't failing a system; he was developing the scientific process in a world that wasn't ready for it. 
> You can’t damage a system that hasn't been born yet

> The bit about Civilization is really interesting. I certainly came up in that milieu. I also strikingly remember talking to a professor at length about Mongol calvary tactics I learned reading the historical reference portions of Age of Empires, and the professor being like 'Why do you know this?' and me being too embarrassed to admit I learned it in a video game. I sometimes wonder at the politics of the moment we're in and whether games like AOE and Civilization have some culpability for unintentionally, and implicitly making the case to several generations of boys that managing a country/culture/civilization is easy, that a single empowered monarchical ruler can bring prosperity and/or dominance, that the masses of humanity are resources to allocate and/or exploit rather than individuals with actual rights,  and that history can be understood as a clash of cultures in a zero-sum game. I definitely feel like there's some "thought-leaders" in the current American rightwing movement politics (looking at you Miller, Musk and Thiel) whom one could argue approach wielding power as being something like a Civ game, and a lot of them are about the right  age and social class to have played Civ a lot as kids.

> 1:58:00 Here's a fun bit of astronomy trivia to go with the Kepler discussions. Often times Kepler's laws are taught with the aid of calculus and Newtonian physics. It makes them very easy to derive and to understand. But Kepler did not have calculus! He did not have Newtonian physics! Newton was born 13 years after Kepler *died*. All Kepler had to work with was Brahe's data and trigonometry. And a deep belief in heavenly perfection: perfect spheres, perfect circles, and so on. And a willingness to throw those ideas away when they did not fit Brahe's data, which is perhaps the most impressive part of all.

> On the topic of censorship, is it possible that miss Palmer's view is skewed by survivor's bias? Since it may very well be that the reason some of the books which have been censored aren't significant in terms of their impact on history is precisely because they were censored. Looking back, it is natural for us to say, "Look at all of these books they censored, none of them had any real impact on the world. They missed all of the important ones." Isn't it possible that some of them would have revolutionized the world, had they not been censored? In other words, isn't it possible that, at least in some instances, the censorship worked? > When it comes to why industrial revolution happened in Europe, I have thought about it myself a lot too, and I think it is a mixture of a lot of factors but also one of luck. By that I mean that Roman Empire chose to spread itself up North because in part of the Sahara desert but also too strong competition in the East, that they could not conquer Parthians, so in a way they had to go for lands in a more shitty climate. Then Christianity spread Roman culture in even shittier climate, as again there was too big competition from Islam in the East... If we look around to other parts of the world, the North largely remained occupied by people who could not build significant civilizations... you had a lot of horsemen in the steppe, but not much in a sense of culture. But you need this same culture to be in the South and North for those people to compete. Like Mongols did not have same culture with the Chinese, so they just subjected Chinese and well they did not have any culture to start with so in time they settled in South and assimilated... In Europe you had Rome and you had Catholicism due to Rome and shared culture. So a king from Sweden or Netherlands may ask - why a Christian king from Constantinople or Italy is better/more wealthy than I am, and he would want to be wealthy too. But due to climate, it was impossibility if you did not invent anything - you would not be able to just outproduce Southern countries doing the same that your father did. So you needed to work your ass to get richer and use your head. While in the East crops grew much more easily and there were no harsh winters making you invest in more sophisticated homes... Also not to forget that Mongol conquest largely spared Europe, that is a big luck factor too... We see that also with Old Russian Novgorod that was in the North and was not sacked by Mongols that could develop quite sophisticated culture, but then Muscovy sacked them...
> In other parts of the world, Northern people just did not have real sophisticated culture, never. Or let's say they did in some Northern parts of Japan or China, but those were never as fragmented in such competing but also sort of brotherly bunch of kingdoms and dutchies etc. that there was competition possible

> There's one particular point where I strongly disagree with Ada, and it's honestly something that runs through her approach to history across the entire interview. 
> 
> The specific point is this: 
> - Around 1:55:00/1:56:00, Ada essentially argues that people in the past that censored content were almost never censoring what they "should have" been really worried about, the seminal texts that to us appear to be the really significant works that marked the watershed of modernity. Fair enough. 
> - But what she underestimates is that for those watershed ideas to have their impact, it was first necessary to destroy the fortress of ideas that were dominant at that point in time. 
> - Catholicism was that fortress in modern France, not the enlightenment, and she underestimates how appealing and strong and influential Catholic ideas were (and still are!). It was THE dominant way of thinking not just among elites but everyone in society and enlightenment ideas were really just common currency among a very small number of eccentric elites at the time, not at all widespread. Rousseau and Voltaire lived in a world that thought their ideas at best amusing and thought provoking, and mostly ridiculous. Even Voltaire is said to have written that Rousseau in his second discourse believes that humans are like dogs that walk on their hands and feet, a comment which was meant to ridicule Rousseau's ideas but today would be seen as scientifically accurate given or current evolutionary way of thinking.  
> - Even when people back then heard those ideas, they weren't much impressed because the dominant seemed more impressive and convincing. Enlightenment ideas really took hold when Catholicism had already been brutally undermined by a series of reform movements from the inside by such ideas as Jansenism and later variants. That's when materialism gained ground and even then by the 18th century people still held broadly to their religious convictions and elites embraced a kind of deism.
> - It wasn't the arrival of powerful ideas but the the destruction of the social, economic, political, and intellectual foundations of catholicism that eventually created the space for those ideas to grow at all. THAT'S WHY THEY CENSORED THOSE PROTESTANT IDEAS. THEY WERE RIGHT! THAT WAS THE THREAT TO THE DOMiNANT WORLDVIEW, NOT THE (arguably weaker) ENLIGHTENMENT VALUES THAT PLAYED SUBSTITUTE WHEN THE FORTRESS WAS DESTROYED! Ada sees those protestant critiques as unimportant because the protestants ultimately won the battle of ideas and she uncritically accepts protestant assumptions as an American from Texas.
> - Now to the broader point about her approach to history writ large: Ada has a tendency to argue that things in the past are much more similar than we think to the modern day, assume a cultural bridge between now and back then. For instance, she talks about Big Wool as an analogy to today's Big Tech, or the difficulty regulating pamphlets as similar to how it is difficult for governments to keep up with hate speech on social media. Again, fair enough. 
> - However, this sometimes vastly underestimates the "cultural" DIFFERENCES that exist between time periods. She assumes that the works of the encyclopedists, or Voltaire, or Lucretius, or Machiavelli are inherently subversive. However, people back then were already well aware of those ideas. They just weren't respected or dominant in society, and that's mostly why they weren't in print, not because people were attracted to them, That came much later when organized religion was in free fall. In fact, she herself admits that people back then, including the inquisitors, were not worried: people aren't learned enough to get this and it's also obviously false. 
> - Our starting point today, Ada's starting point, would be that these works are obviously true and significant. This is our cultural lens, which Ada fails to recognize as such. This was not true then. They weren't even significant enough to be censored. This isn't stupidity on the part of the censors. It's recognition of the real threats to the status quo that permitted later developments. 
> 
> To hammer this home, what Ada is doing is analogous to this: 
> - scholars 400 years from now looking back at what governments censored on social media, like people refusing to accept gender pronouns people attribute to themselves, and think: "These people were so concerned about racist remarks back then, but they really should have been worried about what Transhumanist/Post-humanist ideas being developed in the Silicon Valley that are dominant today (i.e. using tech to transcend human limitations, attributing conscious agency to animals, plants, AI , and so on". But in reality, we know from our vantage point today that people want to censure racist talk on social media because they are deemed a direct attack against a liberal status quo that resting on maximal tolerance and non-discrimination in the context of a democratizing and globalizing society.  It is that worldview that was dominant for decades and that worldview which once destroyed also destroys human dignity and opens up the desire to transgress human limitations, and to attribute consciousness and properly human features to non-human entities. I don't think Ada would say such censorship is really censorship because she thinks those values are relevant, and yet she judges the past like those scholars 400 years from now do, taking for granted battles of ideas that took place back then and assuming things would inevitably lead to materialism and atheism and therefore underestimating how contingent history really is! Our ideas about science and the rise of non-religious ways of seeing the world didn't HAVE to happen, and they can still go away tomorrow. 
> 
> Rant over! :)

It’s always great to converse or hear conversations with people who “GET” history and the interconnections of all cultures and movements and even wars. Of course art history is the best because it comes with pictures of paintings and sculptures!   
>       Many people still do not understand that we are the same as the ancients and have NOT advanced from evolution just by having more technology!  
>      I’m Native and I get colonizer mindset types still telling me that we were all “stone age” and Europeans had to “Give” us “everything.”  One guy (again like so many) tried to say Natives hadn’t invented the wheel to me.  And I rounded on him.  “First of all that is NOT true- there are examples of wheels here- But secondly WHAT HAVE YOU INVENTED?  Why do YOU get to take CREDIT for  all things someone else invented just because your skin matches theirs!?  Did YOU invent Fire?!  Why do you think pale people get to take credit for fire or wheels?  You don’t know.”  
>      Racists genuinely believe pales are more advanced and if they are Mormons- it’s part of their religious doctrine.  
>      And I loved hearing about the Florentine ways of lottery picking to keep royalty away!  I have long said we need a lottery here to get rid of the oligarchs.  It should be “Oh dang- I have to be Mayor this year!  What did you get?  Litter control district manager?  oh not too hard!  And you?  Vice President- yikes well…you can always call your mom if you need help. “

> 
> However i would interpret this differently.
> 
> The billionaires are not nobles, they are the popolos, millionaires and billionaires both are part of this group. they have different amounts of individual power, but the 4-5% control 90% of the wealth in the nation.
> In this sense, the Nobles are in fact the political class, these are senators, presidents, or other political dynasties. You CAN do what you want to those people, because they are of minimal concern, worst they can do is vote or run against you, which wont work if you are broadly supported by the popolos. 
> This is i think what Machiavelli is getting at, the merchant class are (especially in Italy at the time, and today in the west generally) immensely more powerful than any individual noble and perhaps more so than most conceivable collections of nobles. 
> What can the noble do about it if the banker refuses to offer him a loan and the guy who owns the blacksmith closes his doors to him.... not much. Which this i think correlates more closely with what Musk did and the threat we are supposed to perceive from being off side with the popolos.

- author_is_uploader: false

> @Slothreadersclub  Don't you find it strikingly odd that her narrative frames the Renaissance as a kind of "rebirth from nothing," completely overlooking centuries of preservation, translation, and innovation during the Islamic Golden Age and in Al-Andalus? Thinkers like Avicenna, Averroes, Al-Khwarizmi, and Ibn al-Nafis, a 13th-century Muslim physician who first understood the mechanics of the heart and blood long before Western scientists, were instrumental in shaping the very foundations upon which the Renaissance was built.
> 
> Nearly 300 years before William Harvey, Ibn al-Nafis accurately described pulmonary circulation, tracing blood's path from the heart to the lungs and back. He was the first to note that the heart's septum is solid, debunking earlier Greek theories still clung to in Europe, and to recognize the heart as the driving force behind blood movement, essentially identifying its function as a pump. That discovery alone should have rewritten the history books. Instead, she misattributes it to the Renaissance, erasing a monumental achievement in the process.
> 
> And it wasn't just preservation. These scholars expanded, critiqued, and transformed Greek knowledge, then transmitted it across cultures, often via Spain and Sicily, where it flowed directly into the Italian humanist project. To begin the story in 14th-century Florence without acknowledging that intellectual pipeline is like crediting the invention of the smartphone while ignoring the discovery of electricity. The Renaissance didn't emerge from a vacuum: it stood on the shoulders of scholars who kept inquiry alive when Europe had all but extinguished it.

- is_favorited: false
- author_is_uploader: false

> That's the difference between "performative" conversation and "private" conversation (I'm using these terms casually, to talk about this, there's no broader theory):
> 
> in "private" conversations, which are aimed at coming to consensus, discussing, conversing...interruption can be massively helpful and supporting.
> 
> The worst miscommunication is arguably when listeners don't understand while the speaker keeps going on.
> 
> Then, when they finally pause, they find out others haven't been following at all.
> 
> Not only does this waste everyone's time, but it confuses the conversation for everyone, especially the speaker, who no longer has any sense of what's been understood or not.
> 
> There is no perfect compromise between allowing trains of thought to flow, and making sure communication is actually happening.
> 
> For performative conversations meant to be listened to by others,
> 
> interruptions make no sense. Any interruption that would be aimed at helping listeners follow along, can be better directed at asking questions to shift the conversation to be better aimed at them.
> 
> Interrupting serves the interests of limited individuals who are tailoring communication to the present moment.
> 
> There is no need for it when tailoring communication for the masses in the future.
> 
> I find it maddening when folks refuse to interrupt me, and listen silently.
> 
> Often, I find this makes it impossible for us to communicate. I need them to be monitoring whether they're following me, and stopping me when I've begun talking to a brick wall.
> 
> Unfortunately, in most modern communication, people don't want to know how much of what they're saying has been understood as intended. Most of our speech is not seeking understanding. People widely focus primarily on the superficial aspects of language.
> 
> In rhetoric, meaning doesn't matter—only convincing others. Since we use language MUCH more to come to agreement and to argue and reason rather than to seek truth, reality, or understanding,
> 
> those are the most salient meanings of language. The superficial always-untrue heuristic "wrong but useful" connotations dominate, and become what a "reasonable" person can be expected to focus on.
> 
> The language ends up affecting thinking and reinforcing these loops.
> 
> English is such an awful language for true communication...it is great for rhetoric and politics, though. It's good for talking about stuff.
> 
> Saying anything in English requires one to consider when what they're saying is taking place. It's impossible to speak or think in the language without taking time for granted, and treating the illusion of it as real.
> 
> Or course this is basically limiting.
> 
> The solutions exist. Some other languages allow for making statements which have no specified relationship to time.

> ​​ @andygoody2599 If humankind is alive after 1000 years, they still absolutely will view the jump from the Wright brothers plane to Apollo program as enormous, just like we view the invention of the Gutenberg press as very significant. And getting back to the Roman steam engine example - no one viewed it as particularly important at any point in history, including in contemporary times.
> I'm not arguing that humans were less ingenious back then, but it was much harder for them to gain knowledge and to spread the new knowledge that they gained, which made knowledge work extremely inefficient. Adding to that, there were much fewer humans that could even afford the "leisure" of knowledge work. There's absolutely no way these two factors (among others) would not have slowed the rates of technological progress compared to modern times, so anyone claiming that they were in fact the same would have to present some extraordinary evidence in favor of their hypothesis, not just "they were inventing stuff all the time"

> @mirekcolakov1730  Applied linguist here. It's not really about laziness per se. While I think of preserving/using the source-language pronunciation as a sign of respect (and fun!), it is perfectly natural for borrowed words (as linguists call them) and names to be assimilated to the receiving group's sound system. Stress on the second syllable feels more comfortable for English-speakers because of our usual rhythm, stress, and sound patterns. --- Americans don't get upset when Italians say English words or names in an Italian way, especially when they're speaking in Italian. Trying to get an Italian (or French, or Chinese, or Swahili...) speaker to change how they say something to match an American (or British, or Australian...) accent while speaking that other language would even seem offensive in many cases. Also, humans tend to repeat whatever we heard first. And that's generally fine, even if it's different from the way other groups say it.
